title: Herb Scissors Maintenance: Removing Stubborn Stems with a Toothpick
meta_description: Keep your multi-blade shears sharp! Learn the best herb scissors maintenance for removing stems using a simple toothpick and a cleaning comb.
html:
If you've ever used five-blade shears to prep a mountain of cilantro or basil, you know the struggle. They are an absolute game-changer for speed, but they have one glaring weakness: the "stem jam." One thick piece of parsley or a stray woody stem can wedge itself between those precision blades, rendering the tool useless until you clear the debris.

Proper herb scissors maintenance removing stems isn't about expensive sharpening kits; it's about the small, daily habits that keep the blades gliding. While most high-quality sets come with a cleaning tool, sometimes the debris is packed too tight for a comb to reach. That is where the humble toothpick becomes your best friend in the kitchen.

Why Stems Get Stuck in Multi-Blade Shears

Standard scissors have one pivot point and two blades. herb scissors, like the Herb Scissors (Five-blade herb shears that mince cilantro, chives, and basil in one snip — with a cleaning comb), operate on a parallel track. When you cut soft leaves, they slice through cleanly. However, fibrous stems are denser and more elastic.

Instead of being sliced, a stubborn stem can sometimes fold or compress, getting pinched in the narrow gap between the blades. Once one piece of debris is lodged, it creates a "snowball effect," trapping smaller bits of herbs and moisture, which eventually hardens into a sticky residue that prevents the blades from closing fully.

The Toothpick Technique for Removing Stems

When the included cleaning comb can't quite reach a wedge of stem, don't reach for a metal knife or a screwdriver. Using metal tools on your blades can cause nicks or scratches, which lead to rust and dulling. Instead, grab a wooden or plastic toothpick.

Start by opening the scissors as wide as they safely go. Look closely at the blade alignment to find the exact point of the obstruction. Gently insert the pointed end of the toothpick into the gap, working from the outside of the blade toward the pivot point. Use a light prying motion to nudge the stem outward. Because the toothpick is softer than the stainless steel, it will clear the debris without scratching the finish of your shears.

Daily Herb Scissors Maintenance Removing Stems

Prevention is always easier than extraction. To avoid deep-cleaning sessions, implement a quick rinse-and-comb routine every time you switch herbs. If you move from woody rosemary to delicate chives, a quick clear-out ensures the chives don't get crushed by old debris.

  • The Quick Rinse: Run the blades under warm water while opening and closing them rapidly to flush out loose particles.
  • The Comb Sweep: Use the cleaning comb provided with your Herb Scissors to rake through the blades from the base to the tips.
  • The Dry-Down: Never let your shears air-dry in a sink of water. Wipe them down with a microfiber cloth to prevent mineral deposits from creating friction between the blades.

Deep Cleaning for Sticky Residues

Some herbs, like basil or mint, release oils and saps that act like glue. If you find that your blades are "dragging" even after you've removed the physical stems, you likely have a buildup of organic residue.

Fill a small bowl with warm, soapy water and a splash of white vinegar. Soak the blade portion of the shears for ten minutes. This breaks down the sticky resins. After soaking, use your toothpick to clear out any loosened gunk from the tightest corners of the hinge. Rinse thoroughly and dry immediately. For an extra layer of protection, a tiny drop of food-grade mineral oil on the pivot point every few months will keep the action smooth.

Choosing the Right Tools for the Job

Not all herbs are created equal. To minimize the need for intensive maintenance, be mindful of what you're cutting. Multi-blade shears are designed for soft-stemmed herbs. If you are dealing with thick, woody stalks of lemongrass or thick cinnamon sticks, stick to a traditional heavy-duty kitchen shear.

By using a tool specifically designed for mincing—like the Herb Scissors with their integrated cleaning comb—you're already halfway there. The comb handles 90% of the debris, and the toothpick handles the remaining 10%, ensuring your tool lasts for years of meal prep without losing its edge.

FAQ

Can I put my herb scissors in the dishwasher?

While many are labeled as dishwasher safe, hand-washing is highly recommended. The high heat and harsh detergents in dishwashers can dull the precision edges and may cause the pivot screw to loosen over time.

How often should I use the cleaning comb?

Ideally, use the comb every single time you finish a bunch of herbs. It only takes five seconds and prevents the "stem jam" from happening in the first place.

What should I do if the blades feel loose?

Check the pivot screw at the center of the blades. Most high-quality shears allow you to gently tighten this screw with a small screwdriver to restore the tension and ensure a clean snip.
